correctedState:
Substantively correct; two corrections to scope and cites.

CITES: `packages/shared/src/agent/pi-agent.ts:7326-7342` (not :7306) and `packages/shared/src/automations/utils.ts:229-232` (not :221-229).

SCOPE — the finding names the smaller half. The matcher gap is not the defect, it is the symptom of a recorded decision; the defect is the missing PRODUCER.

(a) The matcher half is already a decided, tested, diagnosed deviation. `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-29-inert-unit-b.md:155-165` §3 "Three of the nine should not get a matcher" records ConfigChange as `documented, not implemented — our ConfigChange reports runtime session-config keys, not the five settings-file sources`, with the stated cost ("a ConfigChange hook must be catch-all and read `config_keys` itself") and the reason not to fake it ("Matching on `config_keys` would invent a vocabulary the page does not define"). It is surfaced to the author at registration as `plugin.hooks.matcher_never_matches` (`packages/shared/src/plugins/hooks-automation.ts:346-350`) and locked by `packages/shared/src/automations/conditions.test.ts:663-664`. So `getMatchValueForSdkInput` returning `''` is correct behaviour given the payload, not a bug to fix there.

(b) The still-open half is broader and more severe than "the matcher can never match": Nessy's ConfigChange is a DIFFERENT EVENT that shares Claude's name. Claude's fires on settings-file / managed-policy / skill-file changes; Nessy's fires only on runtime session-config commits (`model`, `authType`, `providerType`, `runtime`, `thinkingLevel`). No settings-file edit produces an occurrence at all — so even a catch-all `"matcher": "*"` ConfigChange hook never sees one. That is recorded three times in the generated register (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-29-deviation-register.md:154, :157, :323`) and re-verified at `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-30-reverification.md:109-113`.

(c) Security consequence worth carrying, for a bank fork specifically: `server-managed-settings.md:277` names ConfigChange hooks as the mechanism to "log modifications or block unauthorized changes before they take effect" for managed policy. With no settings-source producer, that tamper-detection path has nothing to fire on. Separately, hooks.md:717/:2410 make ConfigChange blockable (except `policy_settings`); Nessy's block is advisory only — the config is already committed when the hook runs, documented in-code at `pi-agent.ts:7332-7336`.

STATUS: a known, recorded, OPEN gap with a queued plan slot — `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-30-hook-runtime-contract.md:159` lists it among what that plan leaves, ending "its own plan comes next". Not novel, not refuted, and the producer plan has not been written yet.
